title: Taken
intro: Taken is a 2008 French action thriller film starring Liam Neeson, produced and written by Luc Besson and directed by Pierre Morel. It is the first installment in the namesake film series. Neeson plays Bryan Mills, an American ex-government agent (his former position is never clarified) who starts the series having taken up the job of bodyguard to help pay the bills and attempting to reconnect with

tropes.name: Accidental Murder
tropes.html: Bryan finds Amanda dead the moment she's seen after getting kidnapped, but it's quite clear that this wasn't intended by the Albanians, as they were intending for her to be sold alongside Kim. Her cause of death could be excessive drug use on part of the Albanians.

tropes.name: Always Chaotic Evil
tropes.html: Pretty much ANYONE involved in human trafficking.

tropes.name: Amicably Divorced
tropes.html: Not at the beginning of the film, mind you, but when Bryan single-handedly saved Kimmy's life, he certainly reclaimed a measure of love from his ex-wife, not to mention gaining the friendship and respect of her husband.

tropes.name: Anywhere but Their Lips
tropes.html: After Bryan defends Sheerah against a Loony Fan who tried to kill her, she thanks him afterwards by giving him a talent scout's name for Kim and kisses him on the cheek. While she's slightly older than Bryan's actual daughter, he's still old enough to be her father. In the previous scene, she already cried into his chest the way a distressed daughter might and Kim herself also does later on.

tropes.name: Apologetic Attacker
tropes.html: After coercing Jean-Claude to get information for him by invading his family's home and shooting his wife in the arm, Bryan asks him to convey his apologies to Jean-Claude's wife. The request apparently struck a nerve, as Jean-Claude attempts to attack Bryan, who merely smacks him with a pistol right as the scene cuts.

tropes.name: Armor-Piercing Response
tropes.html: When Brian finally allows Kim to travel to Paris, Lenore asks him if it would have been easier to just sign the foreign travel consent form when he was first asked. Brian then asks if it would have been so hard for him and Lenore to discuss Kim going on the trip instead of dropping it on him out of nowhere, to which Lenore has no response.

tropes.name: Asshole Victim
tropes.html: The Movie. Brian isn't holding back at all when harming people who get in between him and his daughter, repeatedly delivers very brutal beatdown to them, and isn't even above using Jack Bauer Interrogation Technique. However, since his "victims" are all members of sex-slave-trading ring who already played part in kidnapping and enslaving countless innocent women, the more brutal their beating is, the more deserved it actually feels. Special mention goes to Marko, who is tied to a makeshift electric chair, forced to reveal important information, and then just left to die a slow and excruciating death from electrocution. Serves him right. And that's still just a fraction of pain and suffering that he inflicted on others.

tropes.name: Based on a Great Big Lie
tropes.html: One William Hillar, who was eventually revealed to be a fraud who never even served in the military, said that this happened to him in Asia. In his version, it was the friend who survived, not his daughter.

tropes.name: Big Bad
tropes.html: Marko Hoxha, the leader of the kidnappers, and Patrice Saint-Clair, the man who auctions off the kidnapped girls and women. Sheik Raman's bodyguard Ali serves as a Final Boss of sorts, while Sheik Raman himself, as the man who ultimately purchased Kim, is the last person Bryan confronts.

tropes.name: Bullying a Dragon
tropes.html: Marko had no way of knowing exactly who Bryan is, but an organized crime boss should probably recognize that a monotone death threat instead of hysterical pleading (e.g. "I'll pay anything you want!") is going to be trouble, rather than shrug it off like it was nothing important.

tropes.name: But for Me, It Was Tuesday
tropes.html: Strongly implied that everything is just business as usual for the trafficking operation.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• Jean-Claude gives Bryan his card to show that he now works a desk job. Bryan later uses the card to impersonate him when he infiltrates one of the Albanians' brothel.
  • Kim's denim jacket. Bryan finds it with another woman who was also kidnapped and forced into prostitution.
  • The picture of Kim and Amanda that is taken by Peter. Bryan uses it to find Peter and interrogate him.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gunman
tropes.html: Bryan's friend Sam first shows up for a buddy get-together at the beginning of the film. He is later called up to get some information about what happened to Kim and what their best options are.

tropes.name: Compensating for Something
tropes.html: When Bryan and Stewart are arguing, before Bryan has revealed Kim has been kidnapped, and is asking Stewart questions about his business to determine if it had anything to do with Kim being kidnapped, Stewart starts playing the rich guy card, and Bryan yells, "Now's not the time for dick measuring, Steeart!"

tropes.name: Contrived Coincidence
tropes.html:
• The one night Sam hires Mills for a temporary private security job guarding Sheerah just happens to be the one night a crazed fan tries to kill her.
  • Bryan happens to be on the phone with Kim at the precise moment the Albanians break in to kidnap her and her friend; if he'd called her a bit earlier or tried to call a little later, the plot would have ended right there.

tropes.name: Dirty Coward
tropes.html: The young "recruiter" guy, Peter.

tropes.name: Dirty Old Man
tropes.html: Sheik Raman didn't actually want to buy Kim (Bryan forced Ali to do that for the Sheik so he could get the opportunity to save her), but he's more than happy to keep her for himself after the fact.

tropes.name: Dull Surprise
tropes.html: Although he visibly looks horrified, Patrice St. Clair sounds rather relaxed and even kind of sleepy after Bryan wounds him and he attempts to plead for his life.

tropes.name: Electric Torture
tropes.html: Played terrifyingly straight when Bryan does it to Marko. It also averts the trope association of there not being any visible wounding, as the electric current is ran into Marko by nails shoved directly into his thighs. And the scene was edited and censored for the American theatrical release, so the movie would have a comfortable PG-13 rating.note Namely, the jumper cables' place of attachment was changed to the metal of the chair. The original version was restored for the extended edition DVD and Blu-ray releases.

tropes.name: Enhance Button
tropes.html:
One of the clues Bryan follows is a memory card from his daughter's broken cell phone. He finds a picture with a reflection of someone following them around. He doesn't zoom in much, but he is able to enhance it using a contrast and sharpen filter at a kiosk to get a good look at his face.
  • More realistic than usual; most kiosks like that will show a lower-resolution version of the picture to save on loading time. When Bryan presses the "Process" button on the kiosk, it simply loaded the full-resolution picture.

tropes.name: Establishing Character Moment
tropes.html: The first half hour makes it very clear with several things. 1) Bryan loves his daughter more than anything else. 2) Bryan is a stickler for details and does everything with a precise edge to it. 3) He has a past life of undisclosed international field work that leaves him one of the most lethal people on the planet. The rest of the movie is showing what happens when someone takes away the first point.

tropes.name: Fan Disservice
tropes.html: One late scene has Kim in a bikini. Of course, she is underagenote her actress wasn't, thankfully, she is drugged-up, she is being exhibited at a slave auction, and her father is technically being Forced to Watch.

tropes.name: Forced Addiction
tropes.html: The girls kidnapped by the Albanian sex trafficking ring are initially transported to a brothel where they're forcibly drugged. This is meant to make them more compliant and dependent once they're eventually sold onto the black market.

tropes.name: Forgotten Fallen Friend
tropes.html: No one really says anything about Amanda after her death, even Kim herself.

tropes.name: Genre Blindness
tropes.html: If the kidnappers of this film had so much as a shred of savvy, they would've destroyed all evidence by assuring that the SD card got broken along with the cell phone.

tropes.name: Gift for an Outgrown Interest
tropes.html: Subverted. Bryan buys his daughter Kim a karaoke machine for her 17th birthday since she always wanted to be a singer. His ex-wife trivializes it, saying that Kim isn't 12 anymore. Although Kim's stepfather upstages him by buying her a horse, Kim is nonetheless happy with Bryan's present, and is implied to want to pursue a serious music career at the end of the film.

tropes.name: Go-Go Enslavement
tropes.html: With an unpleasantly appropriate justification.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: One of Bryan's most-used techniques when fighting.

tropes.name: Guns Akimbo
tropes.html: Conspicuously subverted, in keeping with the movie's overall practical and grounded approach to combat. Brian acquires a pair of handguns in the climactic gunfight, but he tucks the second one into his waistband and does not draw it until after the first pistol has been emptied and discarded.

tropes.name: Guyliner
tropes.html: One of the Sheikh's men on the boat has this, and he proves to be the toughest of them during his fight with Bryan before he finally goes down.

tropes.name: Happier Home Movie
tropes.html: The movie starts off with Bryan watching a video of Kim's fifth birthday.

tropes.name: Hate Sink
tropes.html: The villains are a bunch of human traffickers, some of the most heinous criminals in the world. And their operations are shown in cold, nightmarish detail for a PG-13 movie.

tropes.name: Hilarity Ensues
tropes.html:
Marko twitching like a cockroach hit by a slipper when Bryan turns on the power. What did that moron expect to happen when he spat at a man who has just slammed two long and rusty nails into his thighs attached to a fuse box?
  • TWICE!!

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html:
Two very brief ones occurs in the film.
  • When Kim is hiding under the bed, she sees the Albanians walking out of the room. She tells Bryan that they're leaving, until she's grabbed.
  • Bryan finds Kim's jacket at the construction site brothel, but not her.

tropes.name: Human Traffickers
tropes.html: The Albanian sex traffickers who kidnap Kim. As Bryan later finds out, however, the Albanians are just part of a larger scale prostitution ring that also includes corrupt French and Swiss officials, and has an Arab Oil Sheikh as one of its customers. Truth in Television: Human trafficking is a $150 billion industry that includes important figures pulling the strings.

tropes.name: I Am Spartacus
tropes.html: When Bryan asks the group of Albanian slavers who Marko is, one of them replies "We are all Marko". However, Bryan tricks the real Marko by asking him to read a note aloud and identifies him by his voice.

tropes.name: I Got Bigger
tropes.html: Kim. The film opens with a home movie of her fifth birthday, and then fast-forwards to her as a 17-year-old (sort of). Plus, this is no doubt what made her so appealing to the sex trafficking scout.

tropes.name: Imperial Stormtrooper Marksmanship Academy
tropes.html:
• Considering the type of movie this is, this trope is unavoidable, but there is one particularly bad case of it at the movie's climax: The Dragon (armed with a sub-machine gun) unloads countless of rounds point blank at Bryan, and all but one bullet miss.
  • Earlier, the Albanians at the construction site unload dozens of rounds into Bryan's vehicle, without a single one hitting him or his passenger.

tropes.name: Instant Death Bullet
tropes.html: If you do not see a shoulder wound, it was a one-shot kill.

tropes.name: Invincible Hero
tropes.html: Throughout the whole entire movie, it seems Bryan's a badass who never gets hit once and everything's going in his favor. However, he does get attacked from behind, gets knocked out, and gets stuck in a trap — from which he quickly escapes and kills everyone there. He does finally meet an opponent with only slightly inferior skills to his own, and beating him finally earns him a good number of scratches and bruises. At the climax he does get winged by several bullets as he hunts down the sheik.

tropes.name: Ironic Echo
tropes.html:
• The phrase "Good luck." Not in the usual way, but perhaps even more badass. Bryan tricks the man who said it to him over the phone (Marko) into repeating it to him in person, to make sure he got the right guy, before he reveals who he is to the Albanians around him.
  • "I told you I would find you..." Bryan first tells the kidnapper over the phone that he will track him down eventually. When he does, he repeats this line, causing Marko to realize his screw-up and attempt to reach for his gun.

tropes.name: ISO-Standard Urban Groceries
tropes.html: Bryan uses a bag as camouflage to get into the Paris apartment. Jean-Claude also carries home a baguette for dinner.

tropes.name: It Works Better with Bullets
tropes.html:
Bryan visits the Pitrels and demands from Jean-Claude to give him the information he needs. Jean-Claude pulls a pistol on Bryan which he had hidden in the bathroom in an attempt to force Bryan to leave. Bryan, one step ahead, responds by dropping bullets onto the table, revealing he had found the pistol earlier and emptied it. He follows by calling out Jean-Claude on how his large amount of time spent at the desk made him unaware of procedures and tactics regarding his job.
Bryan: That's what happens when you sit behind a desk: you forget things! Like the weight in the hand of a gun that's loaded and one that's not.

tropes.name: Jerk with a Heart of Gold
tropes.html: Sheerah. See Rich Bitch.

tropes.name: Karmic Death
tropes.html: Possibly good luck for the Dirty Coward, since as we see later, it prevented him from being 'interrogated'.

tropes.name: Killed Mid-Sentence
tropes.html: "We can negoti—" *BANG*

tropes.name: Last Chance to Quit
tropes.html: Mills gives the kidnappers a chance to release his daughter without further consequences.

tropes.name: Lifesaving Misfortune
tropes.html: An attractive-looking Swedish tourist named Ingrid managed to strike a conversation with Peter, a handsome local, who offers to share a cab with her. Just then Bryan interrupts their chit-chat and literally drags Peter out before both men runs off, so Ingrid probably had to pay full price for a taxi ride... and was spared a horrible fate from becoming another victim of Human Trafficking.

tropes.name: Look Both Ways
tropes.html: After escaping Peter at the airport by by leaping Off Bridge, onto Vehicle, Peter dashes across the road and is run down by a vehicle going the other way.

tropes.name: Missing White Woman Syndrome
tropes.html: Averted, and arguably a Plot Hole, that if attractive young (white) tourists were disappearing all over Paris it would likely draw lot of attention to the authorities. The scene where Bryan visits the "red door brothel" while impersonating Jean-Claude further solidifies the traffickers are paying bribes for their illegal operation to exist.

tropes.name: Mook Horror Show
tropes.html: Never get between a skilled and deadly father and his daughter.

tropes.name: My Girl Is Not a Slut
tropes.html: Kim's virginity is friggin' plot armor.

tropes.name: Nebulous Criminal Conspiracy
tropes.html: The direct abductors are lowlife thugs from the Albanian mafia, but as Bryan carves his way through Paris to find his daughter, he discovers they're just part of a much wider network existing at all levels of society, including the police and high-placed city officials, with one of its clients being a wealthy Arab oil sheik.

tropes.name: Never Bring a Knife to a Gun Fight
tropes.html: The post-climax confrontation. Sheik Raman has a knife and is holding it to Kim's throat. Bryan has a gun pointed at the Sheik's head. Guess who dies?

tropes.name: No "Police" Option
tropes.html: The movie's plot operates under the idea that the cops had a small window of opportunity after Kim was kidnapped, with Bryan doing the whole job in tracking her down. Bryan does consult some friends in the Paris government for help, only to find some pushback in legal matters as well as their engagement in internal corruption.

tropes.name: Non-Action Big Bad
tropes.html: Marko Hoxha and Patrice Saint-Clair. The former did at least try to get a pistol before Bryan quickly curb-stomped him, but all the latter does is leave his men to do the hard work and then plead for mercy at Bryan after he defeats them.

tropes.name: Not Even Bothering with the Accent
tropes.html:
• When Bryan impersonates Jean-Claude, no one questions why a French policeman has an Irish accent, let alone why one is speaking English.
  • Patrice Saint-Clair's name would suggest he's French, but his accent is distinctly American. Oddly enough, he's played by a Frenchman.
  • Marko the Albanian trafficker, played by Kosovan-French actor Arben Bajraktaraj, inexplicably turns into a Cockney British guy as he's screaming "I don't know!" at the end of the electric torture scene.

tropes.name: Off Bridge, onto Vehicle
tropes.html: When Peter is fleeing from Bryan at the airport, he leaps off an overpass and on to the top of a semitrailer parked underneath.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html:
• The look on Marko's face when Bryan says to him "I told you I would find you." He immediately reaches for his gun, but Bryan slams his face into the table first.
  • Saint-Clair when Bryan gets out of the trap in the mansion. As soon as they exchange looks, Saint-Clair runs for his life. He dies.

tropes.name: Only the Leads Get a Happy Ending
tropes.html: Subverted so you don't feel worried about the sex traffickers' victims. Bryan took out several major figureheads along the way of finding Kim, so it's fair to say the entire organization has suffered a heavy blow by the end of the film.

tropes.name: Outside-Context Problem
tropes.html: Bryan is this to the trafficking ring. A retired covert ops wetwork operative savages their operations, all because they snapped up his daughter while he was listening on the phone and he aims to rescue her no matter who gets in his way.

tropes.name: Playing the Victim Card
tropes.html:
Bryan impersonates a corrupt French police officer to ascertain the identities of his daughter's kidnappers under the pretense of visiting the Albanian gang of sex slavers to discuss future bribes. One of the men has the gall to accuse Bryan of trying to extort them because they're immigrants. Mills immediately shuts this down:
Bryan: I'm extorting you because you are breaking the law. You come to this country, take advantage of the system and think because we are tolerant that we are weak and helpless. Your arrogance offends me. And for that the rate just went up 10%. Do you want to keep negotiating, or do we have a deal?

tropes.name: Police Are Useless
tropes.html: All the French cops are depicted as being inept, in cohoots with the sex traffickers, or both.

tropes.name: Pop-Cultural Osmosis Failure
tropes.html:
Subverted.
Bryan: Who's Beyoncé? [Beat] Just kidding.

tropes.name: Properly Paranoid
tropes.html:
• Bryan is proven absolutely right in every way to have tried forbidding his daughter from traveling overseas. As well, the conditions he sets when he finally allows her to go (regular phone calls and such) are the only reason they had any sort of chance of rescuing her.
  • Liam Neeson has stated that the movie caused some cases of this in real life. People have come up to him and told him they will never send their kids to Europe, which he's not too happy about.

tropes.name: Protagonist-Centered Morality
tropes.html: Bryan comes off this way, as he initially appears to care only about his daughter and doesn't help any of the other victims. Somewhat justified, as he only has a 96-hour window to find his daughter, and stopping to help some of the other girls could cost him valuable time. It's also eventually more or less subverted by the fact that, during the course of the search, Bryan managed to kill off most of the figureheads behind the slaving ring, likely destroying the entire setup.

tropes.name: Prove I Am Not Bluffing
tropes.html: Bryan demonstrates that he is willing to do anything to get his daughter back by shooting the wife of his French police contact and threatening to kill her if he won't cooperate.

tropes.name: Punch-Clock Villain
tropes.html: Patrice Saint-Clair tries to paint himself this way, but fails to convince Bryan.

tropes.name: Race Against the Clock
tropes.html: Sam tells Bryan that he only has 96 hours to find Kim before he never sees her again. He barely makes it while Kim is taken away on a yacht.

tropes.name: Reassigned to Antarctica
tropes.html: It's mentioned that in the past, Bryan left a mission to attend Kim's fifth birthday party (filmed in the video he watches at the beginning of the movie) and got reassigned to Alaska for his actions.

tropes.name: Relationship-Salvaging Disaster
tropes.html: Though Bryan remains divorced from his ex-wife, his heroics in this film put him on much better terms with her and their daughter for the remainder of the franchise.

tropes.name: Rich Bitch
tropes.html:
• Lenore can come across this way at the beginning. She has good reason for not liking Bryan, mainly that he wasn't around due to his career taking out very bad people in the CIA, but she winds up looking spiteful and manipulative instead. She repeatedly tries to distance her daughter from Bryan (thankfully unsuccessful) and flaunt the fact that her new husband is richer and can afford nicer things for Kim. This invokes Disproportionate Retribution when you consider the fact that the woman yells at Bryan for trying to give his daughter a gift on her birthday (an Abusive Parent might deserve that treatment, not a guy who simply worked odd hours). And then children of divorce often play one against the other, so their daughter likely played off the tension to get more out of both of them.
  • Pop star Sheerah initially seems like this when, upon being asked by Bryan if she can give his aspiring-to-be-singer daughter any tips, she responds, "Tell her to pick another career." It's later revealed after Bryan saves Sheerah from an attacker that she meant it as a warning, as a lucrative career in the music industry is "not what everyone thinks it is". She ends up giving the number of her vocal coach and her manager to Bryan when he simply responds, "That's what she wants."

tropes.name: Scary Black Man
tropes.html:
• He appears just long enough to get his ass completely kicked by Bryan (though he manages to escape, unlike his partner Peter, leaving his fate over whether he was able to get away or not ambiguous).
  • Also one of the mooks; he's the only mook on Sheik Raman's boat to give Bryan any trouble before the fight with Ali.

tropes.name: Screaming Woman
tropes.html: A single woman at the chapel screams in horror at the sight of Patrice Saint-Clair's corpse, which had reached the public floor by then.

tropes.name: Serious Business
tropes.html: Apparently, sex slaver Marko values keeping the location of our protagonist's daughter secret more than his own life. He's probably worried that his colleagues would do worse if they found out. Oooooh boy, is he wrong.

tropes.name: Sex Slave
tropes.html: The purpose of the trafficking ring is kidnapping girls to turn into these.

tropes.name: Sex Signals Death
tropes.html: Kim is a virgin, as the plot goes out of its way to note. Amanda apparently isn't, and was looking forward to having fun abroad. Guess who dies?

tropes.name: Shoot the Dog
tropes.html: Bryan shoots Jean Claude's innocent wife in the shoulder (non-lethally) to get information about Saint-Clair out of him.

tropes.name: So Beautiful, It's a Curse
tropes.html: For once justified: Kimmy and Amanda are targeted by the Albanians because they're hot and can fetch a lot of money as Sex Slaves.

tropes.name: Spoiled Sweet
tropes.html: Kim is certainly spoiled by her stepfather, but she doesn't short Bryan on some love and hugs at her birthday party (her scream of joy at Stuart's pony gift was louder, but she wasn't faking with Bryan's karaoke machine). This is also in contrast to her mom trying to trivialize his presence.

tropes.name: This Is Gonna Suck
tropes.html: The resigned look on Bryan's face when he tells Kim that she is going to be taken.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html: Kim and Amanda, but mostly Amanda, as Kim had reservations about all the information Amanda was sharing. Two young, pretty American women who don't speak much French go to Paris alone, they accept a car ride with a stranger, they let the stranger see the exact address where they are staying, they tell the stranger where in the building they will be staying, and that they will be alone in the apartment. It's as though they went down a checklist of things not to do when traveling. Amanda is literally too dumb to live and pays the ultimate price for stupidity. Kim, on the other hand, is merely drugged and roughed up, and by the second film she has learned her lesson, as she travelled abroad with both of her parents at the beginning.

tropes.name: Translation Convention
tropes.html: Bryan Mills walks around Paris addressing people in English, including when he's impersonating a French officer. It's implied that he's really speaking French.

tropes.name: Try and Follow
tropes.html: Done semi-successfully by one of the mooks Bryan tracks down.

tropes.name: The Unseen
tropes.html: The entirety of Amanda's family. Her parents are never seen, mentioned or even spoken to via phone; and she says her cousins in Paris have gone on holiday for months, leaving the apartment for her and Kim. This applies even after Bryan finds Amanda's dead corpse, so it's entirely possible that by the end of the film her family still haven't noticed she's missing.

tropes.name: Unwilling Suspension
tropes.html: Bryan gets caught by Patrice Saint-Clair during an auction of prostitutes and is hung by his wrists in this manner, but he soon gets out and overpowers his captors immediately.

tropes.name: Wealthy Yacht Owner
tropes.html: The climax takes place on a yacht, whose owner can afford to shell out hundreds of thousands of dollars for virgin sex slaves.

tropes.name: Villains Want Mercy
tropes.html:
• While Bryan tortures the name of who bought Kim from Marko, he demands where he can find him. Marko repeatedly says he doesn't know, to which Bryan goes to turn on the power for a third and last time. Marko screams in terror that he really doesn't know, and practically begs Bryan to the point of tears not to kill him. It fell on deaf ears.
    Bryan: Where can I find him?
    Marko: (softly between breaths) I don't know, I don't know... (Bryan runs to the power switch) I don't know, I don't know! PLEASE! I DON'T KNOW! I DON'T KNOOOW! NOOO, PLEASE! Please! Please don't do it, please...
    Bryan: I believe you... but it's not gonna save you. (turns on the power and leaves Marko screaming in agony)
  • After Bryan defeated all of Patrice Saint-Clair's men by killing them or knocking them off, the unarmed Patrice practically pisses his pants the moment Bryan angrily stomps towards him with a loaded gun. He begs Bryan not to kill him by claiming that his job of prostitute seller is only business and Nothing Personal towards anyone; Bryan answers by saying It's Personal just before repeatedly plugging him with bullets.

tropes.name: What the Hell, Hero?
tropes.html: A mutual accusation between Bryan and Lenore regarding Kimmy's Paris trip. Lenore called him out for crushing her dream almost on the spot, while Bryan told her off for making it a double-team ordeal where he was the bad guy by default.

tropes.name: Writer Behind the Times
tropes.html: Kim and Amanda are teens who leave to follow the European tour of U2, a band that was much more popular with people 20 years older than them.

title: National Treasure: Book of Secrets
intro: National Treasure: Book of Secrets is a 2007 Disney adventure film that is the sequel to the first adventure. Both director Jon Turtletaub and producer Jerry Bruckheimer return for this production. After the Templar treasure was found, Ben Gates (Nicolas Cage) and his father are well-respected historians making rounds at various universities and lectures. During one of their lectures, Mitch Wilkin

tropes.name: Artistic License – History
tropes.html:
• The film contains a very common misconception. Ben states that Dr. Samuel Mudd, a co-conspirator in Lincoln's assassination, is who the expression "His name is mud," is referring to. This is actually not correct, as the phrase was used at least two decades before Lincoln's assassination.
  • They get the Resolute desks wrong. For one, there were at least three desks made, not two. One is in the White House, one is in the New Bedford Whaling Museum in Massachusetts, and one is part of the Royal Collection. None are used by Queen Elizabeth II. Furthermore, none of the desks were identical: the White House one is a large partner's desk, the museum one is a smaller lady's desk, and the third one is a writing table.
  • Queen Victoria is portrayed as secretly sympathetic to the Confederate cause, but in fact the Queen issues a statement of neutrality that neither helped the Union nor recognized the Confederacy as a sovereign nation. In private correspondence, she sought to continue good relations with both sides, not appearing to favor one over the other.

tropes.name: Bat Deduction
tropes.html:
Ben, yet again. He gets called out on it this time by Abigail, who is tired of him always considering himself right.
Ben: If I'm right after I assume I'm right, then I'm correct.
Abigail: When you get to a conclusion without asking, and you happen to be right, you got lucky.
Ben: I get lucky a lot.

tropes.name: Beta Couple
tropes.html: Ben's divorced parents, Patrick and Emily, in Book of Secrets. They turn out to have split up for similar reasons to Ben and Abigail - once the adventure was over, they had a hard time getting along. It doesn't last.

tropes.name: Black-Tie Infiltration
tropes.html:
Ben gatecrashes the President's birthday party at Mount Vernon so he can get him alone in a secret area of the estate and convince him to let Ben see the President's Book.
Ben: Maybe one day, I'll wear this to a party I'm actually invited to.

tropes.name: Blatant Lies
tropes.html: The President when he said, "What book?" to Riley.

tropes.name: City of Gold
tropes.html: Cibola, the famous city of gold, is the MacGuffin Location for the second film.

tropes.name: Collapsing Lair
tropes.html: Deconstructed, the ancient buried treasure is discovered just in time for massive amounts of water to flood in, forcing the heroes to run for it. It seems like it will be a classic 'discover the treasure only for it to then be lost to the world forever' ending...and then cut to one of the main characters cataloging items in the now-drained treasure chamber. Because unlike a lot of hidden treasures, which are in places like forgotten temples in the middle of nowhere, THIS treasure is buried right in the middle of the United States, under a national landmark, and it's the 21st Century. Of COURSE they can just re-excavate it!

tropes.name: Contrived Coincidence
tropes.html: What are the odds the President would be having a birthday party, giving Ben an opportune moment to speak to him about The President's Book? Depending on whether the party was held on his birthday or merely at some point within a week of his birthday, 1/365 or 1/52, or in layman's terms slightly worse than the odds of getting a straight or three-of-a-kind respectively in poker.

tropes.name: Country Switch
tropes.html: The Australian/Japanese Blu-ray release of Book of Secrets is forced to display Japanese menus and sets the movie to play in English with Japanese subtitles if the disc is played in a region A player. When played on a region B player, the user is allowed to choose between English or Japanese on disc start-up.

tropes.name: Destroy the Evidence
tropes.html: One of the clues, a plank with glyphs pointing to Cibola, was already removed from its hiding spot in the White House's resolute desk. President Coolidge had the plank photographed, translated, and subsequently burnt during his presidency, subsequently commissioning Gutzon Borglum to build Mount Rushmore to hide the remaining markers.

tropes.name: Disposable Fiancé
tropes.html: Connor, the White House guy.

tropes.name: Dying Clue
tropes.html: At the end of the prologue, Thomas Gates tells his son Charles "The debt that all men pay" while dying from gunshot wounds inflicted by Michael O'Laughlin. This turns out to be the answer cypher that leads Ben and Riley to a clue in Paris.

tropes.name: Enemy Mine
tropes.html: This is enforced by the villain himself after he takes Mrs. Gates hostage—Ben has the second half of the coded message thanks to the Book of Secrets, but the villain has the last extra clues needed to find the hiding place thanks to a letter his ancestor received from Queen Victoria. Thus they have to work together both to spare Mrs. Gates' life and have all the needed clues.

tropes.name: Family Honor
tropes.html: While this appears to some degree in the first movie (finding the Freemason treasure will prove that the Gates family was right and weren't just crazy treasure-hunting loons), it is much more directly a motivation in the sequel, where finding the City of Gold will prove why Gates' ancestor had his name on a page in the Booth diary (because the conspiracy appealed to him to crack the code for them) and thus exonerate the family of being connected with Lincoln's assassination.

tropes.name: French Jerk
tropes.html: Subverted, for a change, as two French police officers help translate a clue for Ben and Riley.

tropes.name: Funny Background Event
tropes.html: When Riley is discussing the Book of Secrets in front of the White House, the men on top of the White House in the background are real Secret Service snipers keeping eyes on the film crew.

tropes.name: Landmarking the Hidden Base
tropes.html: Invoked for Mount Rushmore. It is said from a document that it was deliberately made to hide a clue.

tropes.name: Lemming Cops
tropes.html: The car chasing them out of the Library of Congress get stuck on a barrier.

tropes.name: Match Cut
tropes.html: The film features a dissolve between the dome of St. Paul's Cathedral in London and the Capitol Dome in Washington D.C.

tropes.name: Meeting-the-Parents Sequel
tropes.html: Ben's father was already significant to the plot of the first film, but in the sequel, his mother joins the cast too. Since his parents are divorced, this is a recipe for trouble.

tropes.name: Never Trust a Trailer
tropes.html: The Book of Secrets, despite containing all the nation's best-kept secrets, is actually not the major goal of the movie. It's really just a small piece of a bigger puzzle.

tropes.name: Nice Job Breaking It, Hero!
tropes.html: In a Deleted Scene, Patrick accidentally caused the flooding in the caverns beneath Mount Rushmore when he opens a door and water starts flowing past him and Emily, leading to Cibola almost getting flooded and Mitch drowning.

tropes.name: Our Presidents Are Different
tropes.html: Bruce Greenwood as the President. More specifically, Greenwood is a President Personable, and is depicted as being a genuinely noble person who is sympathetic to Gates's quest.

tropes.name: Riddle for the Ages
tropes.html: After being told the titular Book of Secrets exists by no less than the President himself, Ben is asked to look at Page 47 for something not specified. The audience is never shown what exactly the page holds, but Ben tells him at the end that its contents are "life-altering."

tropes.name: Sequel Hook
tropes.html:
• The film has one in the form of "Page 47."
  • Back when there were plans for a third film, the writers stated they wanted the next sequel to be about "Area 51", or Atlantis. It's worth noting that Riley mentions at one point that his book contains secrets regarding both topics. So, it's clear the writers were laying the groundwork for a 3rd film, and Riley's book was serving as Chekhov's Gun.

tropes.name: Sequel Reset
tropes.html:
The Gates family reputation, restored by finding the Templar treasure, is once again ruined by the revelation about the Booth diary, forcing Ben to find another treasure to clear the family name. (Riley didn't get the fame and respect the Gateses did, though, due to being just the assistant; this time around he finally gets some proper recognition). And Ben and Abigail broke up, only to fall in love and get back together again. Lampshaded by Patrick:
"For one brief moment, the Gates family could hold its head up. Now we're a bunch of crazies."

tropes.name: Shout-Out
tropes.html:
When Ben sticks his hand into an opening, he plays a prank reminiscent of Roman Holiday.
Ben: (feels around for a minute, then suddenly yells) GHAAAAH!
Everybody else: GAAAAAH!
Ben: Sorry, couldn't resist.

tropes.name: Signature Item Clue
tropes.html: Invoked by Abigail when she deliberately drops one of her earrings in the Oval Office, then uses that as a distraction for Ben to examine the President's desk, on the grounds that it wouldn't do for an earring belonging to her to be found there.

tropes.name: Status Quo Is God
tropes.html: Riley gets audited and loses his fortune so he actually has a reason to tag along. He gets the car back thanks to a pardon from the President but ends up crashing it five seconds after starting it up because he didn't check which gear it was left in.

tropes.name: Throw the Dog a Bone
tropes.html: Riley spends much of the movie being unrecognized for his role in the Templar Treasure adventure (and various other Butt-Monkey situations). In the end, he meets a pretty fan of his who recognizes him from his book.

tropes.name: Who Shot JFK?
tropes.html: It's written in the President's Secret Book.

title: Evil Dead
intro: Mia has a problem. For years, she has struggled with a heroin addiction that has come close to killing her, and her friends have decided to stage an intervention. After everyone meets in a remote cabin, they tell Mia that they will be staying there until she is fully detoxed. Unfortunately, this particular cabin has its own history with demons of a more supernatural sort, and her friends haven't l

tropes.name: Bait-and-Switch
tropes.html: The entire Cold Open. We're set up to sympathize with the girl being hunted by what appear to be villainous country folk, only to then find out that said girl is possessed by a Deadite and previously killed her mother, and the kidnappers are doing so at the request of her father, who wishes to put his beloved daughter out of her misery.

tropes.name: Beauty Is Never Tarnished
tropes.html:
• Crosses over with Beauty Equals Goodness; after David buries Mia alive to drive the Evil out of her, the horrific wounds she'd sustained in her demonic form disappear.
  • Years of drug abuse don't seem to have affected Mia's looks much, either (aside from a slightly unkempt appearance and a pale complexion).

tropes.name: Bilingual Bonus
tropes.html: One of the phrases written in the Naturom Demonto, "Sono Tutti Morti", means "They Are All Dead" in Italian.

tropes.name: Bittersweet Ending
tropes.html: Mia survives and kills The Abomination but her brother, their dog, and her friends are all dead and she ends up losing her hand. Also the book is still out there.

tropes.name: Blasting It Out of Their Hands
tropes.html: Along with Call-Back, where David shoots Natalie's entire hand off as she's about to kill Eric.

tropes.name: Bloodier and Gorier
tropes.html: Oh yes. The gore is much more detailed and realistic than the original by a longshot. If you post any gory scene from the 1981 original on Reddit, they'll accept it fine. But post any gory carnage from this film and the site will automatically mark it NSFW.

tropes.name: Breaking Old Trends
tropes.html: For the first time in the franchise, there is a Final Girl.

tropes.name: Break Them by Talking
tropes.html: The deadite possessing Mia gives David this lecture for abandoning his sister and his dying mother years ago.

tropes.name: Bring My Brown Pants
tropes.html: When Olivia starts to lose control and become possessed, she openly urinates on herself.

tropes.name: Broke Your Arm Punching Out Cthulhu
tropes.html: Literally, Mia had to amputate her own hand to get the chainsaw to kill the abomination.

tropes.name: Call-Back
tropes.html: The film has several to the original film, including Sam Raimi's Oldsmobile parked outside the cabin, Deadite Cheryl's death threat being heard during Mia's possession, and Professor Knowby's original tape recording playing during the credits.

tropes.name: The Cameo
tropes.html: Bruce Campbell as Ash appears in a post-credits scene.

tropes.name: Cannot Kill Their Loved Ones
tropes.html:
• David prepares to burn the cabin while his possessed sister Mia is locked in the cellar. He is ultimately unable to go through with it.
  • Subverted in the "live burial" scene. David wrestles with burying his (still) possessed sister as she tugs at his heartstrings, but this time actually does it. However, this is what frees Mia from the evil spirit when David revives her.

tropes.name: Chekhov's Gun
tropes.html:
• The meat saw Natalie uses at the beginning of the film which she later uses to saw off her arm to avoid being possessed.
  • The nail gun they used to fix the broken door later gets used as a weapon.

tropes.name: Darker and Edgier
tropes.html: After an increasingly comedic trilogy, this film is fairly jarring in tone. It edges pretty close to Torture Porn as the main characters mutilate themselves and each other, the teenagers aren't at the cabin for a party, it's nearly devoid of jokes or one-liners, and it's entirely lacking the original trilogy's camp value. Granted, it's likely the film was specifically meant to be a remake of the first film, which actually was straight horror. Supported by the fact that the film refers to the Necronomicon as the "Naturom Demonto", which is what it was called in the original film.

tropes.name: Deadpan Snarker
tropes.html:
Mia.
Olivia: No, come on, slumber party isn't over yet.
Mia: Yeah, we still haven't played “Fuck, Marry, Kill”, right?

tropes.name: Decoy Protagonist
tropes.html: The film seems to set up David as the new expy of Ash from the original film, from his clothing to the amount of focus he receives in the story, but after he's killed, it's Mia who takes on the Ash role in the end, losing her hand, dispatching the Abomination with a chainsaw, and being the only character to survive the ordeal. Neatly played with, as Mia is actually the film's first victim, so audiences wouldn't expect her to become the only one left at the end, at least, not until David successfully exorcises the demonic force from her.

tropes.name: Diabolus ex Machina
tropes.html: The movie seems to be closing out after David successfully resuscitates and exorcises Mia and the two finally hug it out after being at each others throats all movies. Only for a deadite-possessed Eric to appear, kill David, and complete the ritual to summon the Abomination.

tropes.name: Double Standard: Rape, Female on Female
tropes.html:
• Averted. The scene where the possessed Mia pulls Natalie into the cellar and begins licking her legs, then splits her own tongue with a knife and force-kisses Natalie is just as sickening and violating as it should be.
  • Averted very hard too when Mia becomes entangled in the vines in the forest and a female looking demon (appears as Mia herself) vomits up a black, thorny, tentacle like creature that slithers up Mia's leg and rapes her, going completely inside of her. It is not even remotely erotic or comedic but absolutely terrifying and disturbing.

tropes.name: Duct Tape for Everything
tropes.html: David uses duct tape for first aid to tape gauze onto a stab wound, wrap up an amputation site, and in the makeshift defibrillator he uses to revive Mia.

tropes.name: Evil-Detecting Dog
tropes.html: Grandpa, Mia's dog, sniffs out the trapdoor to the cellar.

tropes.name: Evil Laugh
tropes.html: Deadite Mia gets a very quiet and menacing one.

tropes.name: Expy
tropes.html: In the end, we get an evil version of Mia, which seems to be the Bad Ash of the new series.

tropes.name: Eye Color Change
tropes.html: Characters' eyes change color when they are possessed. Most notably, Mia's change color right before she tackles Olivia.

tropes.name: Flat Character
tropes.html: Natalie gets the least depth and development of the group.

tropes.name: Foreboding Carcass
tropes.html: While David and Eric are searching in the basement to find out what smells down there, they come across dozens of dead, mummified cats hanging from the ceiling. They find a book down there which they will unfortunately read from and accidentally summon an evil entity that causes all of the cabin dwellers to hurt and attempt to kill themselves and each other.

tropes.name: Foreshadowing
tropes.html: Early in the film, Olivia tells David that the last time she and Eric tried to help Mia get clean, Mia relapsed, overdosed, legally died for a bit, and had to be revived. This sets up David killing Mia by burying her alive, then reviving her.

tropes.name: Forging Scene
tropes.html: David rigging the hypodermic needle-defibrillator.

tropes.name: Genre Blindness
tropes.html:
Eric is the one who decided to unwrap a package wrapped in garbage bags and barbed wire. Even after he realizes the book is bound in human skin and has very apparent warnings that the book shouldn't be tampered with including:
Don't say it, Don't write it, Don't hear it!
  • Ironically enough this same character is the first one to realize and come to terms with what is really going on when thing start going to hell. Granted this is mostly due to the knowledge gained from having read the ill-fated book, as well as knowing that his reading from the book was the reason it all started.

tropes.name: Going Cold Turkey
tropes.html: Mia’s friends brought her to the cabin to help her kick her heroin addiction.

tropes.name: Groin Attack
tropes.html: A rare female example when Mia is possessed, her possession being caused by some kind of sentient intertwined thorns that are vomited up by a demonic vision of herself. The thorns slide their way up Mia's leg and into her vagina. It is certainly not played for laughs and clearly a very violating and painful moment.

tropes.name: Hard Truth Aesop
tropes.html: Sometimes you have to do the hard thing for the best results. This is generally the theme of the group's plan as a whole for coming to the cabin, in that quitting drugs cold turkey is notoriously difficult to pull off and viciously hard on the quitter, but they hope for it to be more effective than rehab has been for Mia. Eric usually suffers the most when confronted with the Deadites, but he fights back instead of trying to run away; thanks to this, he lives a little longer, and is able to save David from the Deadites twice when he could've tried to escape. David himself is castigated by the others for running away and leaving Mia to care for their mother. Most aggressively, Mia is forced into a Life-or-Limb Decision to survive and vanquish the Abomination, wherein the choice to be made is an awful and hideously painful one, but will allow her to survive. Subverted with Natalie, though, as cutting off her arm doesn't save her at all.

tropes.name: Heroic Sacrifice
tropes.html: David gives up his life to save Mia from Deadite Eric. Turns into Stupid Sacrifice right after when we learn that this fifth death fulfills the conditions for the abomination to enter our world, leaving Mia all alone against a much greater threat. Possibly Played Straight since David was quickly bleeding out and Deadite Eric's "He's coming" line implies the conditions were already met.

tropes.name: Here We Go Again!
tropes.html: After Mia survives and walks away from the cabin, the Naturom Demonto is ominously shown being blown closed by a gust of wind.

tropes.name: Hope Spot
tropes.html: Natalie looks like she's made it out of the cellar, despite the broken step, until Mia grabs her ankle at the last second and drags her back down.

tropes.name: Humanoid Abomination
tropes.html: The creature that rises up from hell in the finale, which is basically a lanky demonic form of Mia. It's even called "The Abomination."

tropes.name: Licking the Blade
tropes.html: Taken to extremes, when Mia licks a utility knife and then presses her tongue into the edge hard enough to slice her tongue in half down the middle.

tropes.name: Life-or-Limb Decision
tropes.html:
Subverted, then played straight near the end.
  • Cruelly subverted with Natalie, who cuts off her arm but ends up possessed anyway.
  • Played straight with Mia, who has to rip off her hand to reach the chainsaw and defend herself.

tropes.name: Loophole Abuse
tropes.html: The only way to cleanse someone of the Evil is the kill them via immolation, dismemberment, or live burial. However, with careful planning and an improvised Magical Defibrillator, David manages to exorcise Mia and successfully bring her back to life.

tropes.name: Made of Iron
tropes.html: Eric, full stop. Shard of glass in the chest, needle to the face, shot multiple times in the arms and chest with a nailgun, crowbar to the hand, crowbar to the head, and he STILL risks his life trying to save his friend.

tropes.name: Magical Defibrillator
tropes.html: David shocks Mia back to life with a car battery charger wired to a pair of syringes.

tropes.name: Meaningful Name
tropes.html: Sort of. The first letters of each of the characters' names spells D.E.M.O.N.

tropes.name: Oh, Crap!
tropes.html: Natalie's face when she realizes Mia has just grabbed her ankle.

tropes.name: Our Zombies Are Different
tropes.html: Deadites are undead created via Demonic Possession, and far from being mindless, shambling corpses, they are downright malicious, being fond of self-mutilation and tormenting their prey. They also gain sickly yellow and red irises and disturbing, demonic voices.

tropes.name: Rain of Blood
tropes.html:
During the climax of the film, it starts to rain blood as David's death was the final one needed for the ritual that brings about the Abomination.
  • This scene alone utterly shattered Braindead’s record of largest amount of fake blood used in a film production, a record that film had held on to for over 20 years! Braindead had used around 1,000 gallons. This sequence used fifty times that amount!

tropes.name: Rasputinian Death
tropes.html: Eric is on the receiving end of one throughout most of the film. He first falls and hits his head on the sink with enough force to break it, suffers a stab wound on his chest dangerously close to where his heart ought to be as well as multiple stabs from a syringe to the face, the needle breaking off and becoming embedded dangerously close to his eye. Some time later he gets attacked with a nail gun and gets more than a few in his arms, body and face. Soon after he gets attacked with a crowbar and gets his hand smashed almost in half trying to block it, as well as getting a few full blows directly to his head. Despite this he still manages to make his way to the basement from the outside and save David from the possessed Mia, at which point she stabs Eric fatally.

tropes.name: Revisiting the Roots
tropes.html: The Evil Dead was a pretty straightforward horror movie with little humor, and the campy Bloody Hilarious-Horror Comedy elements came in more and more in the sequels. This film just goes back to the mood of the first film.

tropes.name: Senseless Sacrifice
tropes.html: David's death, while removing Deadite Eric as a possible threat to Mia, otherwise succeeds only in making the fifth and final sacrifice to summon the Abomination.

tropes.name: Sliding Scale of Comedy and Horror
tropes.html: In the overall franchise that's known for being comedically scary, this movie swings straight into comedy-free horror, even more than the original film. The original film plays the horror straight has a ton of unintended comedy because it visibly shows that it had a very small budget. This movie plays the horror straight with the budget and technology evolution to make it much more gruesome.

tropes.name: Spiritual Antithesis
tropes.html: To the preceding Evil Dead films thanks to its Darker and Edgier tone, eschewing the Horror Comedy elements of Evil Dead 2 and Army of Darkness in favor of unflinching gore and brutality that's played deadly seriously.

tropes.name: Stealth Sequel
tropes.html:
If one takes The Stinger with its appearance of Ash seriously, this means that this is a sequel to the original Evil Dead trilogy, just involving some new victims getting into the same mess that Ash did so long ago. This is confirmed in a line in Evil Dead Rise as it's explained that the book discovered is one of three of the Naturom Demonto.
  • Word of God states that this movie and Ash vs. Evil Dead, an official sequel to the original trilogy, do indeed take place in the same universe, and that the creators like the idea that Mia might pop up in the series eventually, or Ash might make more than a cameo in a future movie.

tropes.name: Supernatural Gold Eyes
tropes.html: Watch out for yellow eyes.

tropes.name: Surprisingly Realistic Outcome
tropes.html: A very minor example during the Deadite attack in the bathroom. Deadite Olivia viciously goes for Eric's eye with a syringe. Not only does the needle not make it through his glasses lens, but it breaks off and gets embedded off-target, completely averting the expected Eye Scream. Syringes, as it turns out, aren't knives and will break if mishandled.

tropes.name: The Stinger
tropes.html: Ash appears at the end of the credits to say one of his signature lines. "Groovy".

tropes.name: Trailers Always Lie
tropes.html: The trailer includes several clips that don't appear in the finished movie, including David messily attacking someone with a chainsaw and Mia chanting the possessed Linda's song from the original. Later averted when in 2016 an "Unrated Cut" surfaced with the cut scenes put back in.

tropes.name: Tome of Eldritch Lore
tropes.html: The Book of the Dead, here called "Naturom Demonto" like in the original film instead of "Necronomicon Ex Mortis", the name used in later ones.

tropes.name: Too Dumb to Live
tropes.html:
• Eric. Seriously, the amount of shit he has to blithely go through to unleash the Evil — cutting open barbed wire, ripping open a garbage bag, then painstakingly etching to get the magic words that have been painstakingly scribbled out, all while ignoring scribbled warnings against doing just that — is just ridiculous.
  • After arriving at the cabin, Eric and David explore the basement, which not only has dozens of rotting cat corpses hanging from the ceiling, but also a very scorched support beam, suggesting that somebody was burned there. Instead of freaking out and leaving the place, they react with Dull Surprise, and instead set about cleaning out the ritualistic dead cats.

tropes.name: [Verb] This!
tropes.html: "Feast on this, motherfucker!" just before shoving the chainsaw into the Abomination's mouth.

tropes.name: Vomit Indiscretion Shot
tropes.html: Mia does this twice. When the cravings are getting to her, she's outside the cabin walking around in circles, she vomits after a while. Later when she gets possessed, she projectile vomits blood all over Olivia.

tropes.name: You Cannot Grasp the True Form
tropes.html: Mia gets several looks at the Force (the disembodied thing flying around the woods), and sees a demonic version of herself. Later, just before Olivia gets possessed, she sees a similarly monstrous version of herself in the mirror. "The Abomination" may also count, as Mia is the only one there to see it and it looks somewhat like her, or it could just be that the Abomination took the form of the first person to be possessed.
